## From the repo

### Intent
What this repository is for, from its .zbuild/vision.md. It steers every
choice you make.


### zBuild — Vision

> The North Star for zBuild — it steers how zBuild is built. The README distills it; the wiki references it; every pipeline run is steered by it.

#### Intent
zBuild turns a delivery process into data — templates and plugins — so software is built the same disciplined way every time. We build zBuild the way zBuild builds: a minimal core, with all behavior plugin-delivered and template-composed. A good change is small, aligned to the spec, proven by a test, and wired into the live path — never scaffolding that looks finished but does nothing.

#### Principles
- **Target-agnostic by contract** — zBuild builds *any* repository, not itself; the engine and plugins never assume the target's language, layout, or that zBuild is the target. Target knowledge lives in data — templates, config, per-repo overrides — never in code.
- **Spec wins over drift** — KEEPERS, ARCHITECTURE, and the ADRs are the source of truth; when code disagrees, the code changes, not the spec.
- **Small engine, behavior at the edges** — keep the core tiny; add capability as plugins composed in templates, never by growing the engine.
- **Safety is structural** — all model-bound text passes one redaction chokepoint; state is atomic and resumable; scope is governed at every boundary.
- **Models are data, not code** — selection flows through the router and config tiers; never hardcode a model name.
- **Prove behavior, then wire it** — every change ships a test that fails without it and connects to the live path; green-but-inert is a defect.
- **Fail closed, never silent** — gates block on real problems and say why; bounded cycles and recovery drive work to done.
- **Dogfood every change** — build zBuild with zBuild; if the pipeline can't ship it, fix the pipeline.

### Rules
These are this repository's rules (.zbuild/prompts/rules.md). Work that
breaks one is wrong, whoever wrote it.

- Bash only, and match the file you are in: 4-space indent, LF line endings, a final newline, no trailing whitespace (.editorconfig). Everything must pass `shellcheck` with the repo's .shellcheckrc.
- Never pipe anything into `grep -q`, and never pipe into a bare `head`, in any `.sh` file, test files included. The reader exits early, the writer takes SIGPIPE, and under `set -o pipefail` the line fails for a reason nothing logs. Use a here-string instead: `grep -q PATTERN <<< "$var"`, or run grep on the file directly: `grep -q PATTERN "$file"`. `tests/unit/sigpipe-antipattern-guard-test.sh` fails the suite on any violation; a genuinely safe pipe is annotated `# sigpipe-ok: <reason>`.
- Never name a model (haiku, sonnet, opus, …) in code; model selection goes through core/router and config/models.json.
- A test must be able to fail: assert what is required, never what the code happens to do.
- Never edit anything under `legacy-DoNotUse/`.

#### Facts about this repo
- `ZBUILD_*` environment variables are set by the engine at dispatch (the artifact dir, the stage's input index `ZBUILD_STAGE_INPUTS`, the issue, the run). They are trusted engine inputs, not user or attacker input.
- A stage never names another stage's output — not its output name, not its file. The engine hands every stage every earlier stage's latest output, and a stage finds what it needs by what it contains (scripts/lib/earlier-output.sh; ADR-055 §1). A plugin that names another stage's output is a defect.
- Every stage writes a v2 result (`result_contract`, `verdict`, `disposition`, `reason`, detail under `data`) on every exit path, and exits 0 or 1 (ADR-054).
- `[SPEC-n]` / `[#<issue>/SPEC-n]` tags in a test tie an assertion to one issue's acceptance contract. A tag that belongs to another issue must never be changed or removed.

## What you own

Your job: for each finding below, try to show that it cannot happen. Read the
code each finding names, what calls it, and what feeds it its input. A finding
stands unless you can quote code that shows it cannot happen on a real run —
its trigger never occurs, or something already stops it. Judge only these
findings: add none of your own.

Answer one line for each finding, by its number:

<n>: stands
<n>: knocked down | WHY: <why it cannot happen> | QUOTE: <file> | <one line of the code that shows it>

Copy each QUOTE as it is, with no quote marks around it: it is checked, and a
knock-down whose quote is not there leaves the finding standing.

THE FINDINGS:
### 1
file: core/pipeline/runner.sh
severity: high
message: After zbuild_claim_acquire succeeds, the two early-failure return paths — _runner_enter_worktree failure and zbuild_run_branch_setup failure — call only zbuild_run_cap_release and return before the EXIT trap is installed (line 2940), so zbuild_claim_release is never called; the zbuild:claimed label stays on the issue permanently until removed by hand.
trigger: A network outage or git error causes _runner_enter_worktree or zbuild_run_branch_setup to fail on a run that already acquired the claim; the process exits with no EXIT trap set, the label stays, and every subsequent run on the same issue is refused until an operator removes the label by hand.
quote: if ! _runner_enter_worktree "$state_dir" "$_runner_run_id" "$_wt_key"; then         zbuild_run_cap_release || true         return 1     fi

### 2
file: core/claim/claim.sh
severity: medium
message: _ccgl_read_holder selects the last GitHub comment that contains the substring <!-- zbuild-run-status and extracts whatever the zbuild-holder field says; any user who can comment on the issue can craft a comment that becomes the most-recent match, injecting attacker-controlled content into the error message printed to the operator's terminal.
trigger: An outside actor posts a comment on the issue whose body contains the string <!-- zbuild-run-status and a crafted <!-- zbuild-holder: EVIL --> line; the next refused run prints the crafted string verbatim (including terminal escape codes) in the error logged to the operator's shell.
quote: body="$(gh issue comment list "$issue" --json body \                 --jq '[.[] | select(.body | contains("<!-- zbuild-run-status")) | .body] | last' \                 2>/dev/null || true)"

### 3
file: plugins/claim-coordinator/github-labels/plugin.sh
severity: low
message: Despite the design decision explicitly stating 'plugin.sh must not source core/claim/claim.sh — that would create a circular dependency and add a startup $(cd …) subshell in plugin.sh's load path', the change adds exactly that at the bottom of plugin.sh; the || true guard silently swallows a cd failure and lets pwd produce the working directory, so the resolved path and hence the sourced claim.sh would be wrong whenever BASH_SOURCE[0] is empty.
trigger: plugin.sh is sourced in a context where BASH_SOURCE[0] is empty (eval, process substitution, or any non-file source path); cd silently fails, pwd returns the current working directory, and the constructed path ../../../core/claim/claim.sh resolves relative to that directory instead of the plugin's location.
quote: _ccgl_plugin_dir="$(cd "${BASH_SOURCE[0]%/*}" 2>/dev/null || true; pwd)"

Based on reading `core/pipeline/runner.sh`, `core/claim/claim.sh`, and `plugins/claim-coordinator/github-labels/plugin.sh`, here are my verdicts:

---

**Finding 1 — the claim-acquire-to-trap gap in runner.sh**

`zbuild_claim_acquire` is called at the block starting "Cross-machine soft claim via zbuild:claimed GitHub label (ADR-005 / #1764)." The two early-return paths that follow it — the `_runner_enter_worktree` guard and the `zbuild_run_branch_setup` guard — each end with `zbuild_run_cap_release || true; return 1`. Neither calls `zbuild_claim_release` or `zbuild_issue_lock_release`. The EXIT trap (`trap '_runner_abort_trap' EXIT`) is installed further down in main(), at line 2940, well after these return statements. `_runner_abort_trap` is the only function that calls `zbuild_claim_release`. A failure on either early path exits with the claim label still on the issue and no mechanism to remove it.

**1: stands**

---

**Finding 2 — attacker-controlled holder string via GitHub comment**

`_ccgl_read_holder` in `core/claim/claim.sh` (gh branch) issues `gh issue comment list "$issue" --json body --jq '[.[] | select(.body | contains("<!-- zbuild-run-status")) | .body] | last'`. It then walks the body line by line, matching `^'<!-- zbuild-holder: '(.+)' -->'$`, and prints `${BASH_REMATCH[1]}` verbatim. No sanitization is applied before or after. The return value becomes `_ZBUILD_CLAIM_HOLDER`, which runner.sh passes directly to `error "issue … is already claimed: ${_ZBUILD_CLAIM_HOLDER:-unknown}"`. Any user who can post a GitHub comment containing `<!-- zbuild-run-status` and a crafted `<!-- zbuild-holder: … -->` line controls what appears in that error message, including ANSI escape sequences.

**2: stands**

---

**Finding 3 — BASH_SOURCE[0] empty when plugin.sh is sourced**

The trigger requires `BASH_SOURCE[0]` to be empty inside plugin.sh at the moment the `$(cd "${BASH_SOURCE[0]%/*}" ...)` subshell runs. On every real run, plugin.sh is loaded by exactly one code path: `claim.sh` line 17 issues `source "${_ZBUILD_ROOT}/plugins/claim-coordinator/github-labels/plugin.sh"`. When bash executes a `source` command with a filename argument, it sets `BASH_SOURCE[0]` to that filename inside the sourced file. `BASH_SOURCE[0]` is empty only when code is evaluated without a file — via `eval` or a here-string `source /dev/stdin` — neither of which occurs in zBuild's production path. The `cd` therefore succeeds; the `|| true` is never exercised; and the constructed path resolves correctly.

**3: knocked down | WHY: plugin.sh is always loaded via a file-path source in claim.sh, so BASH_SOURCE[0] is never empty inside plugin.sh on a real run | QUOTE: core/claim/claim.sh | source "${_ZBUILD_ROOT}/plugins/claim-coordinator/github-labels/plugin.sh"**
